content: 1. The acceptance rate for tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT) was reported to be 81% when using moxifloxacin (MFX) or ofloxacin (OFX), and Malik et al. found an 80% acceptance rate for levofloxacin (LFX) or MFX combined with a companion drug such as ethambutol (ETH) or pyrazinamide (EMB). However, this acceptance rate decreased when TPT regimens were associated with potential side effects. 2. Studies investigating the willingness of caregivers and household contacts (HHCs) of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) patients to initiate hypothetical fluoroquinolone-based TPT were conducted in various countries, including Botswana, Brazil, Haiti, India, Kenya, Peru, South Africa, and Thailand. Among 299 caregivers of children under 13 years of age, 93% were willing to administer daily TPT pills to their children, and 95% were willing to complete the necessary steps to determine eligibility for MDR-TPT. 3. Two studies evaluated the willingness and ability to adhere to a novel child-friendly levofloxacin (LFX) formulation for TPT. Purchase et al. reported high acceptability among children and their caregivers, with 81% of caregivers finding the formulation easier to prepare than the adult version and 82% finding the tablet size acceptable. Similarly, Wademan et al. found high acceptability but noted concerns among caregivers about financial and caregiving burdens, particularly when they were also undergoing treatment for MDR-TB. 4. A cost-effectiveness analysis by Dodd et al. demonstrated that providing TPT with screening and treatment for co-prevalent TB disease was more cost-effective than focusing solely on detecting and treating disease among HHCs of MDR-TB patients. Targeting high-risk groups, such as children under 5 or under 15 years with HIV, was the most cost-effective strategy. Providing TPT to all children under 15 years of age averted the most deaths and achieved the greatest reduction in disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) lost. Updated analyses incorporating efficacy estimates from the TB CHAMP and V-QUIN trials yielded similar results. 5. No randomized controlled trials addressing the objectives of the systematic review were identified, and thus, no high-quality evidence on the efficacy of fluoroquinolone-based TPT for MDR-TB contacts was available. Observational studies had limitations, including selection bias and small sample sizes, and none demonstrated significant benefits of fluoroquinolone-based TPT in preventing MDR-TB disease. However, larger observational studies suggested that fluoroquinolone-based TPT is safe, with no grade 3, 4, or serious adverse events reported for LFX or MFX. Fluoroquinolone monotherapy showed high completion rates and acceptability, with only mild to moderate adverse events observed in children and adolescents. 6. A high-quality modeling study evaluating cost-effectiveness found that targeting the highest-risk groups, such as children under 5 or under 15 years with HIV, was the most cost-effective approach. However, providing fluoroquinolone-based TPT to all contacts under 15 years of age had a greater impact and remained more cost-effective than focusing solely on detecting prevalent TB disease. Higher-quality evidence is needed to assess the efficacy of fluoroquinolone-based TPT in preventing MDR-TB disease among contacts. 7. A qualitative study assessed the acceptability of levofloxacin (LFX) as TPT for adult household contacts of MDR-TB patients in five lowand middle-income countries: Georgia, India, Indonesia, South Africa, and Vietnam. Eligible participants were identified, and interviews were conducted to explore their attitudes, values, and perspectives on using fluoroquinolones as TPT. Participants were informed about the risks of MDR-TB disease, the differences between TB infection and disease, and the risks and burdens of MDR-TB treatment, including treatment duration, adverse events, and outcomes. This allowed participants to make informed decisions about their preferences for TPT versus the increased risk of developing MDR-TB disease. 8. The acceptability of TPT for MDR-TB depended on whether participants valued disease prevention, perceived the effectiveness, requirements, and safety of TPT as meeting their subjective thresholds, and anticipated being able to complete the treatment successfully. Sociocultural and economic contexts, as well as personal and community experiences with MDR-TB, influenced participants' values. Those who valued disease prevention and trusted medical professionals were more likely to accept TPT. However, some participants who did not value disease prevention refused TPT regardless of its potential benefits. 9. Participants who accepted TPT were willing to tolerate mild-to-moderate side effects and long treatment durations if the treatment had a minimum level of efficacy, such as reducing the risk of disease by 50%. Safety was prioritized over treatment duration, while the treatment schedule was considered the least important factor. Perceived feasibility, including the demands of TPT on daily life, transportation, clinical follow-ups, time commitments, childcare arrangements, and financial and social support, also influenced acceptability. 10. Overall, MDR-TPT was found to be acceptable and held high social value among participants in the five settings. The most acceptable regimen would have high effectiveness in preventing MDR-TB, mild toxicity, minimal interference with daily activities, low pill burden, convenient clinical follow-ups, and low cost to participants.
